why_how.text: Every new driver passes the Driving Knowledge Exam first and then has two years to complete the Driving Skills Exam.
The examiner checks the vehicle's registration, insurance, lights and seat belts before the skills exam begins.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on Washington's two driving exams. Every new driver must pass both of them: the Driving Knowledge Exam, which checks your understanding of Washington's rules of the road, and the Driving Skills Exam, which checks your ability to apply those rules. In this lesson we cover the order of the exams and the time window between them, who may be in the car during the skills exam, what the vehicle must have, and where you can take the exams. These are practical rules that decide whether your exam can even begin.

lines.text: Then two years for the skills exam.

narration.text: The order is fixed. The knowledge exam must be passed first, and from that point you have two years to complete the skills exam. So passing the knowledge exam does two things at once. It unlocks the skills exam, and it starts a two-year clock. The skills exam can never be taken first, so there is no way around this order. The simplest plan is to book the skills exam well inside the two years after you pass the knowledge exam. To remember: knowledge exam must come first; then two years for the skills exam. A helpful hook for this lesson: knowledge first, then two years for skills.

During the skills exam, only you and the examiner may ride in the vehicle. The guide makes two exceptions: service animals and sign language interpreters. So a parent, a friend or your driving instructor cannot come along for the ride, even to keep you calm. The examiner is there to watch how you apply the rules on your own. If someone besides the stated exceptions is in the car, the exam cannot go ahead as described. Plan for any passengers to wait outside the vehicle while you test. To remember: only you and the examiner; exceptions: service animals; exceptions: sign language interpreters.

lines.text: Working brake lights, signals, seat belts.

narration.text: The vehicle you bring is part of the exam. It must be legally licensed and registered. It must carry proof of current liability insurance that names the policy holder or describes the vehicle. And it must have working brake lights, signal lights and seat belts. The examiner verifies every requirement before the exam begins, so a burnt-out bulb can stop the test before you leave the lot. Checking your lights and paperwork the day before is a simple way to protect your appointment. To remember: licensed and registered; proof of current liability insurance; working brake lights, signals, seat belts.

Here is the trap. Some learners assume the two exams can be taken in either order, or that a strong driver could take the skills exam first. The guide is clear: the knowledge exam must be passed first, and the skills exam can never be taken first. Passing the knowledge exam then opens a two-year window for the skills exam. If a question offers the skills exam as the first step, it is wrong. The knowledge exam always opens the door, and the two-year clock starts when you pass it. To remember: knowledge exam always first; two-year window starts then.

The knowledge exam comes first, and it starts a clock for the second exam. The answer is two years. Passing the knowledge exam opens a two-year window for the skills exam, and the skills exam can never come first. When the learner is ready to book, they can test at an approved driver training school exam location or through a licensing office appointment. A helpful hook for this lesson: knowledge first, then two years for skills.

lines.text: Knowledge first, two years for skills.

narration.text: To wrap up, every new driver passes the Driving Knowledge Exam and then the Driving Skills Exam, with two years to complete the skills exam after passing the knowledge exam. Only you and the examiner ride during the skills exam, apart from service animals and sign language interpreters. The vehicle must be licensed, registered and insured, with working brake lights, signal lights and seat belts. You can take the exams at an approved driver training school exam location or book an office appointment in License Express.

Untrained drivers over eighteen face a higher crash risk, which is why adult courses exist.

narration.text: This lesson looks at driver training across a lifetime. For new drivers under eighteen, approved driver training is the standard path. For adults who never took training, some schools offer traffic safety courses. And for older drivers, the guide explains how changing abilities, rather than age, should guide decisions about driving. We will cover what each kind of training includes, who it is for, the parent orientation that teen courses must provide, and how drivers can respond to changes in vision, fitness and reflexes.

Approved driver training for new drivers under eighteen combines two parts: classroom lessons and behind-the-wheel training from a licensed instructor. It is offered by private schools and by some school districts. Courses for students under eighteen must also offer a parent orientation class. That class explains the practice-driving requirement of forty daylight hours and ten night hours. So the parent is brought into the process early, and knows exactly how much supervised practice the teen will need before licensing.

lines.text: Untrained adults face higher crash risk.
Also for anyone wanting a refresher.

narration.text: Adults are not left out. Drivers over eighteen who never took driver training face a higher crash risk. For that reason, some schools run adult traffic safety courses. They serve three groups: beginners, newcomers to the United States, and anyone wanting a refresher. So an adult who learned informally, or who learned to drive in another country, has a structured option. The guide presents these courses as a response to the higher crash risk of untrained adult drivers. To remember: untrained adults face higher crash risk; courses for beginners and newcomers; also for anyone wanting a refresher.

lines.text: Myth: a set age ends driving.
Assess, adjust, or choose other transport.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many people think a certain birthday should end a person's driving. The guide disagrees. Age alone should not decide whether someone keeps driving. What matters are changes in vision, fitness and reflexes, which can raise safety concerns. Drivers should assess those changes and either adjust their habits or choose other transportation. So the right answer to a question about older drivers focuses on abilities and adjustments, not on a fixed age limit. To remember: changing abilities raise concerns; assess, adjust, or choose other transport.

Here is a quick check: a driver training course enrolls students under eighteen. What must it offer the students' parents? Think first. The course combines classroom and behind-the-wheel training, and the parents play a role in the practice that follows. The answer is a parent orientation class. That class explains the requirement of forty daylight hours and ten night hours of practice driving, so parents know what they will be supervising and attesting to. A helpful hook for this lesson: abilities, not birthdays, guide driving.

To sum up, approved teen driver training combines classroom lessons with behind-the-wheel training from a licensed instructor, offered by private schools and some school districts, and it must include a parent orientation class explaining forty daylight and ten night hours. Untrained drivers over eighteen face higher crash risk, so some schools run adult courses for beginners, newcomers and refreshers. Finally, age alone should not decide who drives; changes in vision, fitness and reflexes should be assessed and met with adjustments.

narration.text: This lesson is about keeping your license current once you have it. The guide covers replacing a lost or damaged license, when you can renew and what happens if you wait too long, how to report a change of address or name, and a few optional registrations you can make when you apply. None of these rules involve driving skill, but they come up in everyday life, and their deadlines and channels are easy to confuse. We will keep each one tied to the right method and the right time limit. To remember: replacing a lost license; renewing on time; updating your record.

lines.text: Replace online at the DOL website.
Or a duplicate at any office.

narration.text: If your license is lost, stolen, destroyed or unreadable, you can replace it online through the DOL website, or get a duplicate in person at any driver licensing office. There is no need to retake exams or wait for your renewal date. The guide offers both channels, online or in person, so you can choose what fits. Keeping a readable license with you matters, and the replacement process is designed to be straightforward for each of those situations. To remember: lost, stolen, destroyed or unreadable; replace online at the DOL website; or a duplicate at any office.

lines.text: Renew up to one year early.

narration.text: Your expiration date is printed near the bottom of the license. You may renew as early as one year before it expires, either online through License Express or at a licensing office. Waiting has a cost. Renewing after expiration may add a fee. And if a license has been expired for eight or more years, renewal is no longer a simple step: you must retake both the skills and knowledge exams. So the safest habit is to check the date on your card and renew within that one-year early window. To remember: expiration date near the bottom; renew up to one year early; online or at an office.

lines.text: Trap: any late renewal is just a fee.
Up to one year early is fine.
Eight or more years expired: both exams.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Learners often treat every late renewal as a matter of paying a fee. A late renewal may add a fee, but the guide sets a hard line further out. You may renew up to one year before expiration, and a license that has been expired eight or more years means retaking both exams. So the two numbers answer different questions. One year tells you how early you may renew. Eight years tells you when a lapsed license sends you back through both the skills and knowledge exams. To remember: up to one year early is fine; eight or more years expired: both exams.

lines.text: Address: License Express within ten days.

narration.text: Changes to your record have their own rules. After a move, you must update your address in License Express within ten days. A name change works differently: it has to be made at a driver licensing office. So the two changes use different channels. The address change is quick and online, with a short ten-day deadline. The name change requires an in-person visit. When a question describes a change, first decide whether it is an address or a name, and the channel follows from that. To remember: address: License Express within ten days; name: at a licensing office.

lines.text: Register to vote online or at an office.
Ages sixteen and seventeen may pre-register.

narration.text: The guide also lists some optional registrations. You can register to vote at the Secretary of State's website or at a licensing office, and residents aged sixteen and seventeen may pre-register when they apply for a license or ID card. When applying for a license or ID card, you may also register with the U.S. Selective Service System, and you may say whether you are a twin for the state research registry. These are choices offered at the licensing counter, not requirements for getting your license. To remember: register to vote online or at an office; ages sixteen and seventeen may pre-register; selective Service and twin registry.

Here is a quick check: a driver's license expired eight years ago and they now want to renew. What must they do? Work it out before the answer. A short lapse may add a fee, but this one has reached the eight-year line. The answer is that they must retake both the skills and knowledge exams. A license that has been expired eight or more years means retesting. Had they renewed on time, they could have done it up to one year early, online or at an office. A helpful hook for this lesson: address online in ten days; name in person.

lines.text: Renew up to a year early.
Address in ten days; name in person.

narration.text: To close, replace a lost, stolen, destroyed or unreadable license online or as a duplicate at any office. Renew up to one year before expiration; late renewal may add a fee, and eight or more years expired means retaking both exams. Update your address in License Express within ten days of moving, and make a name change at a licensing office. When you apply, you can also register or pre-register to vote, register with Selective Service and join the twin registry. To remember: replace online or in person; renew up to a year early; address in ten days; name in person.

narration.text: This lesson covers how driving privileges can be lost and what it takes to get them back. The guide lists many grounds, from breaking intermediate license restrictions to serious crimes involving a vehicle. It also sets a special rule for minors who commit alcohol, drug or firearm offenses. Finally, it explains what reinstatement requires. These lists are long, so we will group them: rule-breaking and violations, risky driving, and serious offenses, followed by the minor's delay and the steps back to a license. To remember: grounds for losing privileges; a minor's license delay; getting a license back.

lines.text: Minor with alcohol, drugs or firearms.

narration.text: The first group of grounds is about rules and records. You can lose driving privileges for breaking intermediate license restrictions, for a minor possessing alcohol, drugs or firearms, for piling up moving violations, and for driving while suspended or revoked. Each of these is listed in the guide as grounds for losing privileges. Notice that some apply only to young drivers, like the intermediate restrictions, while others, like driving while suspended, apply to every driver. To remember: breaking intermediate restrictions; minor with alcohol, drugs or firearms; piled-up violations; driving while suspended.

lines.text: Fleeing police, DUI, racing, reckless driving.
Assault, homicide, hit and run, uninsured.

narration.text: The next grounds involve risky or serious conduct. Privileges can be lost for fleeing police, driving under the influence, racing or reckless driving, endangering a construction or emergency worker, or letting traffic citations go unresolved. Further grounds are vehicular assault, vehicular homicide, hit and run, a felony involving a vehicle, driving uninsured, and failing a competency evaluation. So the list runs from paperwork, like unresolved citations, to the most serious crimes a driver can commit. To remember: fleeing police, DUI, racing, reckless driving; endangering road workers; unresolved citations; assault, homicide, hit and run, uninsured.

lines.text: License can be delayed until seventeen.

narration.text: Minors face an extra consequence. A minor who commits an alcohol, drug or firearm offense risks having the license delayed until age seventeen. This can happen even before the minor holds a license, because the delay pushes back when a license may be issued. It is a separate rule from the impairment limits for drivers under twenty-one. The delay is about an offense committed as a minor, and its age marker is seventeen, not twenty-one. To remember: alcohol, drug or firearm offense; license can be delayed until seventeen.

lines.text: Trap: the delay runs to twenty-one.
Covers alcohol, drug, or firearm offenses.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because the guide has several rules for drivers under twenty-one, learners sometimes stretch the minor's license delay to age twenty-one. That is wrong. A minor's alcohol, drug or firearm offense can delay the license until seventeen. The under-twenty-one rules are different: they are impairment limits that apply while driving. So if a question asks how long a minor's offense can delay a license, the answer is seventeen. Keep twenty-one for the impairment limits. To remember: offense delay: until seventeen; under twenty-one limits apply while driving.

lines.text: Pay a reissue fee plus usual fees.
Under eighteen: parent or guardian consent.

narration.text: Reinstatement takes real effort. To get a license back, you must retake the knowledge and skills exams, even if you passed them before. You must pay a reissue fee on top of the usual fees. And if you are under eighteen, you need a parent or guardian's consent. So a lost license does not simply return when a suspension ends. The driver goes back through both exams, pays an extra fee, and, for minors, brings a parent or guardian back into the process. To remember: retake knowledge and skills exams; pay a reissue fee plus usual fees; under eighteen: parent or guardian consent.

lines.text: Retake them to get the license back?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver lost their privileges and wants the license back. They passed both exams years ago. Do they need to retake them? Decide first. It is tempting to think earlier passes still count. The answer is yes. To get a license back you must retake the knowledge and skills exams even if you passed them before. You also pay a reissue fee on top of the usual fees, and a driver under eighteen needs a parent or guardian's consent. A helpful hook for this lesson: offense as a minor: wait until seventeen.

To finish, privileges can be lost for breaking intermediate restrictions, a minor possessing alcohol, drugs or firearms, piled-up violations, driving while suspended, fleeing police, DUI, racing or reckless driving, endangering road workers, unresolved citations, and serious offenses such as vehicular assault, homicide, hit and run and driving uninsured. A minor's alcohol, drug or firearm offense can delay a license until seventeen. Getting a license back means retaking both exams, paying a reissue fee and, under eighteen, parent consent.

narration.text: This lesson covers Washington's law on driving under the influence. Washington law makes it illegal to drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and it reaches further than many people expect. We will look at what the law covers, including physical control of a parked vehicle, then the Implied Consent Law, and finally the limits for alcohol and THC. Those limits change with age, and the difference between drivers twenty-one and older and drivers under twenty-one is one of the most tested ideas in this section.

Washington law makes it illegal to drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs. A second section of the law also covers being in physical control of a vehicle, even a parked one. Physical control means being able to take control of the vehicle's engine or operation. So both situations fall under the DUI law, in two separate sections. A person does not have to be moving down the road for the law to apply. Being impaired while able to control the vehicle is enough. To remember: illegal to drive impaired; physical control counts too; even in a parked vehicle.

Next is the Implied Consent Law. Under it, anyone who drives in Washington has agreed to be tested whenever an officer suspects alcohol or drug impairment. The agreement comes from the act of driving here, not from a separate form you sign at the roadside. That is why refusing a test has its own consequences, which the next lesson covers. For now, remember the core idea: by driving in Washington, you have already consented to impairment testing when an officer suspects it. To remember: driving here means you agreed; tested when impairment is suspected.

lines.text: Twenty-one and older: point zero eight.
Same consequences at the lower level.

narration.text: Now the alcohol limits. A blood alcohol concentration of zero point zero eight percent or higher is DUI for drivers aged twenty-one and older. Drivers under twenty-one face the same consequences at zero point zero two percent. So the younger limit is the stricter one, and the consequences are the same once it is reached. The guide's limits table lists these levels side by side: adults at zero point zero eight percent or more, and minors under twenty-one at zero point zero two percent or more. To remember: twenty-one and older: point zero eight; under twenty-one: point zero two; same consequences at the lower level.

lines.text: Twenty-one and older: more than five nanograms.

narration.text: THC follows the same pattern, but more sharply. More than five nanograms of active THC per milliliter of blood is DUI for drivers aged twenty-one and older. Drivers under twenty-one face the same consequences for anything above zero nanograms. That makes the under-twenty-one rule a zero-tolerance rule. Learners often apply the adult cannabis limit to younger drivers, but younger drivers have no allowance at all. Any active THC above zero brings the same consequences as a DUI. To remember: twenty-one and older: more than five nanograms; under twenty-one: anything above zero; zero tolerance for younger drivers.

lines.text: Trap: one limit for all ages.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many learners memorize the adult numbers and apply them to every driver. For alcohol, the adult limit is zero point zero eight percent, but drivers under twenty-one face DUI consequences at zero point zero two percent. For THC, adults are limited above five nanograms per milliliter, but drivers under twenty-one face consequences for anything above zero. So whenever a question gives an age under twenty-one, switch to the stricter rule: the lower alcohol level and zero tolerance for THC. To remember: under twenty-one: stricter alcohol limit; under twenty-one: zero THC tolerance.

Here is a quick check: a twenty-year-old driver has a small amount of active THC in their blood, well under five nanograms. Does that bring DUI consequences? Think it through. Five nanograms is the adult limit, but this driver is under twenty-one. The answer is yes. Drivers under twenty-one face DUI consequences for anything above zero nanograms of active THC. That is the zero-tolerance rule, and it is why the adult limit never applies to younger drivers. A helpful hook for this lesson: adults point zero eight; under twenty-one, point zero two and zero THC.

lines.text: Adults point zero eight; minors stricter.

narration.text: To close, Washington law makes it illegal to drive under the influence of alcohol or drugs, and it also covers physical control of a vehicle, even a parked one. Under the Implied Consent Law, anyone who drives in Washington has agreed to be tested when an officer suspects impairment. For drivers twenty-one and older, the limits are zero point zero eight percent alcohol and more than five nanograms of THC. For drivers under twenty-one, they are zero point zero two percent and anything above zero. To remember: driving or physical control; implied consent to testing; adults point zero eight; minors stricter.

A DUI conviction can bring a suspension of ninety days to four years plus an ignition interlock and other conditions.

narration.text: This lesson covers the consequences of impaired driving. Under the Implied Consent Law you have already agreed to testing, so refusing a test carries its own penalty. Then there is the driving record, where alcohol and drug offenses stay for life. And a DUI conviction can bring a long list of penalties, from a suspension and an ignition interlock to reapplying for a license. The suspension ranges for refusal and for conviction are close enough to confuse, so we will compare them directly. To remember: refusing a test; a lifetime record; conviction penalties.

lines.text: Ninety to seven hundred thirty days.
Or until twenty-one, whichever is longer.
Length depends on factors like prior violations.

narration.text: Refusing a test can cost your driving privilege for ninety to seven hundred thirty days, or until you turn twenty-one, whichever is longer. The length within that range depends on factors such as how many violations you have. So refusing is not a way to avoid consequences. It brings a suspension of its own. For a younger driver, the until-twenty-one part of the rule can make the suspension longer than the day range alone. Keep this range for refusal separate from the conviction range. To remember: ninety to seven hundred thirty days; or until twenty-one, whichever is longer; length depends on factors like prior violations.

lines.text: Offenses stay on your record for life.
Arrest: license loss and heavy fines.

narration.text: Alcohol and drug offenses stay on your driving record for life. A DUI arrest can also bring license loss, heavy fines, criminal penalties, jail time and higher insurance rates. So the costs of a DUI do not end when a suspension ends. The record follows the driver permanently, and the financial and legal costs can be serious. When the guide lists these consequences, it is describing what can follow a single arrest, not only repeated offenses. To remember: offenses stay on your record for life; arrest: license loss and heavy fines; criminal penalties, jail, higher insurance.

lines.text: Suspension of ninety days to four years.

narration.text: A DUI conviction can combine several penalties. It can bring a suspension of ninety days to four years together with a probationary license, an ignition interlock device, proof of financial responsibility, and an alcohol assessment and treatment report. A conviction can also require you to reapply for a license, retake the knowledge and skills tests, and pay the reissue fee. So after a conviction, a driver may have to rebuild their license from the beginning, with extra conditions attached. To remember: suspension of ninety days to four years; probationary license, ignition interlock; financial responsibility; alcohol assessment.

lines.text: Trap: refusal and conviction ranges match.
Refusal: ninety to seven hundred thirty days.

narration.text: Here is the trap. The refusal suspension and the conviction suspension both start at ninety days, so learners often assume they are the same. They are not. A test refusal suspension runs ninety to seven hundred thirty days, or until age twenty-one, whichever is longer. A DUI conviction suspension runs ninety days to four years. So they share the same floor but have different ceilings. When a question asks about a range, first decide whether it describes a refusal or a conviction. To remember: refusal: ninety to seven hundred thirty days; conviction: ninety days to four years.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a driver refuses an impairment test after an officer suspects alcohol. Which suspension range applies? Decide before the answer, and be careful, because two ranges in this lesson start at the same number. This is a refusal, not a conviction. The answer is ninety to seven hundred thirty days, or until the driver turns twenty-one if that is longer. The conviction range of ninety days to four years belongs to a DUI conviction, which is a different event from refusing the test. A helpful hook for this lesson: same ninety-day floor, different ceilings.

lines.text: Refusal: ninety to seven hundred thirty days.

narration.text: To sum up, refusing a test can cost driving privileges for ninety to seven hundred thirty days or until twenty-one, whichever is longer. Alcohol and drug offenses stay on your record for life, and an arrest can bring license loss, fines, criminal penalties, jail and higher insurance. A conviction can bring a suspension of ninety days to four years with a probationary license, an ignition interlock, proof of financial responsibility and an assessment, plus reapplying, retesting and the reissue fee. To remember: refusal: ninety to seven hundred thirty days; record: for life; conviction: up to four years, interlock.

rationale.text: Opened alcohol may ride only in the trunk or truck bed, so no compartment within the driver's reach qualifies.

narration.text: This short lesson covers Washington's open container law. It is one of the simplest rules in this section, but it is often misunderstood in two ways: people assume it applies only to the driver, and they assume a closed compartment is a safe place for an opened bottle. We will look at what the law bans, who it covers, and the only places where opened alcohol or cannabis may be carried. By the end, you should be able to place any opened container correctly in a vehicle. To remember: who the law covers; what it bans; where opened items may ride.

lines.text: Anyone in a vehicle on the road.

narration.text: The open container law makes it a traffic infraction for anyone in a vehicle on the road to drink alcohol or use cannabis. It is also an infraction to hold opened or partly used alcohol or cannabis, or to hide either in unlabeled or mislabeled containers. The key word is anyone. The rule covers every occupant, not just the driver. So a passenger drinking from an open can, or holding a partly used container, breaks the law just as a driver would. To remember: anyone in a vehicle on the road; no drinking or using cannabis; no opened or hidden containers.

Here is the trap. Because drinking and driving is about the driver, many people assume the open container law is too. It is not. The law makes it an infraction for anyone in a vehicle on the road to drink, use cannabis, hold opened or partly used alcohol or cannabis, or hide either in unlabeled or mislabeled containers. So a passenger with an open drink is covered. If a question suggests that only the driver is restricted, it is describing the rule incorrectly. To remember: the law covers every occupant; hidden containers are covered too.

lines.text: Only the trunk or a truck bed.
Never a compartment the driver can reach.

narration.text: So where can an opened bottle or partly used cannabis go? Opened alcohol or cannabis may be carried only in the trunk or a truck bed. It may never go in a storage compartment the driver can reach. That rules out the glove box, the center console and any other space within reach, whether it is open, closed or locked. The guide's line is simple: if the driver can reach it, it does not qualify. The trunk or the truck bed are the only allowed places. To remember: only the trunk or a truck bed; never a compartment the driver can reach.

Here is a quick check: a driver has an opened can of beer and wants to put it in a closed center console. Is that allowed? Think it through first. The console is closed, but the driver can still reach it. The answer is no. Opened alcohol may ride only in the trunk or a truck bed, so no storage compartment within the driver's reach qualifies, closed or not. The can belongs in the trunk, or in the bed of a truck. And remember that the same rule binds passengers, since the law covers anyone in the vehicle. A helpful hook for this lesson: opened goes in the trunk.

lines.text: No drinking, cannabis or open containers.

narration.text: To close, the open container law makes it a traffic infraction for anyone in a vehicle on the road to drink alcohol or use cannabis, to hold opened or partly used alcohol or cannabis, or to hide either in unlabeled or mislabeled containers. It covers every occupant, not just the driver. Opened alcohol or cannabis may be carried only in the trunk or a truck bed, never in a compartment the driver can reach. That completes this section on exams and keeping your license. To remember: covers everyone in the vehicle; no drinking, cannabis or open containers; trunk or truck bed only.
